issues.legal_issue: Legislation terminating private coal-mining leases and restricting coal-mining operations falls within Parliament’s legislative competence when it advances the public-interest regulation and development of mineral resources.
material_facts: The challenged amendment terminated most outstanding coal-mining leases, restricted who could conduct coal-mining operations, and allowed public authorities to obtain prospecting licences or mining leases over affected land.
The stated legislative purpose included conserving coal, preventing reckless and unscientific mining, and enabling exploration and planned development before further exploitation.
The continuing statutory duty to conserve and develop minerals applied, and the amendment did not prohibit all future development or working of the mines.
issues.conclusion: Parliament had legislative competence to enact the amendment; it was not a mere device to terminate leases without advancing mineral regulation and development.
issues.legal_principle: Article 246(1), read with Union List Entry 54, gives Parliament power over regulation of mines and mineral development to the extent declared expedient in the public interest. The Court applied the duty of the Central Government under section 18 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, and held that conservation, prospecting, investigation and planned exploitation may serve that purpose even if mining does not resume immediately after leases end. It referred to Attorney-General for Ontario v. Attorney-General for Canada and Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo on regulation and conservation, and applied Julius v. Bishop of Oxford in considering whether an enabling power carries a duty to act with reasonable promptitude in context.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_mining_legis: The proceeding challenges the validity of legislation governing mining operations and leases.
predicates.mineral_regulation_is_under_union_contro: The legislation concerns mineral regulation and development placed under national legislative control in the public interest.
predicates.lease_termination_advances_conservation_: The legislation ends existing leases as part of a scheme aimed at conservation and planned development of mineral resources.
predicates.future_prospecting_or_leasing_remains_po: The legislation leaves prospecting or later mining under new licences or leases possible.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns mining legislation under national control, lease termination advances conservation and planned development, and future prospecting or leasing remains possible, the legislation falls within Parliament’s competence.

issues.legal_issue: A lessee of a composite coal-and-fireclay mine may mine fireclay only if doing so does not involve a coal-mining operation that the lessee is not authorised to conduct.
material_facts: The leases covered mines with alternating seams of coal and fireclay.
The lessees asserted that fireclay could not be extracted without disturbing or mining coal.
The legislation prohibited persons outside specified categories from conducting coal-mining operations and provided penalties for unauthorised mining.

The Court construed the definition of a coal mine in the nationalisation legislation as not encompassing a composite coal-and-fireclay mine, but held that the prohibition on coal-mining operations applied independently of that definition.
issues.conclusion: The composite leases were not wholly brought within the statutory definition of a coal mine, but their holders could not mine fireclay where that operation required mining coal; fireclay mining remained permissible only to the extent it could be done without coal-mining operations.
issues.legal_principle: The Court read section 2(b) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973, alongside section 3(c) of the Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, and the scheme of the nationalisation legislation. It applied sections 3(3)(a) and 30(2) of the 1973 Act, as amended, to hold that the prohibition and penalty for coal-mining operations applied even to a composite lease outside the definition of a coal mine. The Court’s order allowed fireclay mining only so long as it involved no coal-mining operation.

rule.if: challenge_to_mining_restrictions and composite_mining_lease and operator_is_outside_authorised_categories and fireclay_extraction_requires_coal_mining

predicates.challenge_to_mining_restrictions: The proceeding concerns the application of restrictions on mining operations to a composite mining lease.
predicates.composite_mining_lease: The operator holds a lease covering both coal and another mineral in the same mine.
predicates.operator_is_outside_authorised_categorie: The operator is not within a category authorised to conduct coal-mining operations.
predicates.fireclay_extraction_requires_coal_mining: The operator cannot extract the other mineral without also conducting a coal-mining operation.

issues.definition: If a composite-lease holder outside the authorised categories cannot extract the other mineral without mining coal, the holder cannot conduct that extraction.

issues.legal_issue: Terminating surviving coal-mining leases without payment does not violate equal protection when the affected interests differ materially from interests previously taken over and compensated.
material_facts: Earlier legislation provided for management or nationalisation of identified coal mines and for payment of amounts to owners whose management or ownership interests were taken over.
The amendment terminated leases and sub-leases said to have survived the earlier legislation.

The Court found that the affected leaseholders were differently situated from owners whose lawful and identifiable interests had been taken over and compensated; surviving claims were generally precarious or not readily identifiable.
issues.conclusion: The amendment did not violate Article 14 by treating the affected leaseholders differently from owners paid under the earlier legislation.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not require identical treatment of persons who are materially differently situated. The Court considered the payment schemes in the Coal Mines (Taking Over of Management) Act, 1973, including section 7, and the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973, including its acquisition and payment scheme, and distinguished the interests addressed by those Acts from the surviving interests terminated by the amendment. It held that the distinction did not amount to unequal treatment.

predicates.equal_protection_challenge_to_lease_term: The proceeding alleges unequal treatment arising from legislation terminating mining leases.
predicates.earlier_acquired_interests_were_identifi: Earlier takeovers concerned identifiable interests for which the legislation provided payment.
predicates.terminated_surviving_interests_were_mate: The interests terminated later were materially different from the identified interests taken over earlier, including because they were precarious or not readily established.

issues.definition: When terminated surviving interests are materially different from earlier identifiable interests for which payment was provided, the different treatment does not violate equal protection.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory termination of mining rights is an extinguishment rather than a compulsory acquisition when the terminated rights do not vest in the State and any new State interest requires a separate positive step.
material_facts: The amendment terminated most existing coal-mining leases and sub-leases but did not provide that the terminated interests vested in the State.
After termination, a public authority could apply for a prospecting licence or mining lease; obtaining a new interest required a further positive step.
The Court found that interests acquired under the earlier management and nationalisation legislation had been paid for, while the amendment extinguished any surviving right to win coal.
The challenge alleged that the amendment acquired property or mining businesses without payment and unjustifiably restricted property and business rights.
issues.conclusion: The amendment extinguished the surviving mining rights rather than acquiring them for the State, and Article 31A(1)(e) protected it from being invalidated under Articles 14, 19 and 31; the challenges based on acquisition, property and business rights therefore failed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 31A(1)(e), a law providing for extinguishment or modification of mineral rights is protected from invalidity under Articles 14, 19 and 31. Article 31(2A) distinguishes compulsory acquisition from deprivation that does not transfer ownership or a right to possession to the State or a State-controlled corporation. The Court applied Dwarkadas Shrinivas v. The Sholapur Spinning & Weaving Co. Ltd. on examining substance rather than form, and distinguished Ajit Singh v. State of Punjab and Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India because the terminated interests did not vest in the State. It also relied on the statutory payment schemes for interests acquired under the earlier management and nationalisation legislation.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_termination_: The proceeding challenges legislation that ends mining rights on property or business grounds.
predicates.terminated_rights_do_not_vest_in_the_sta: The legislation ends the existing rights without transferring those rights to the State or a State-controlled entity.
predicates.a_new_state_interest_requires_a_separate: A State entity must take a further affirmative step to obtain a new licence or lease after the existing rights end.

issues.definition: If terminated mining rights do not vest in the State and a new State interest requires a separate positive step, the termination is an extinguishment rather than compulsory acquisition.
